hook: This woman could not stop dancing.
visual_style: Stylized 3D animated film look, soft rounded shapes, smooth clean surfaces, bold saturated colors, strong rim light, period-accurate detail, warm amber and deep red palette
world: Strasbourg, summer 1518: a cobbled medieval square of half-timbered houses, dusty summer sun by day, torchlight at night
through_line: the cobbled square, fuller of dancers with every block until it empties at dawn

cast.Frau Troffea: a thin woman in her 30s, auburn hair under a white linen coif, plain red woollen dress with a laced bodice, bare feet
cast.Magistrate: a stern older man, short grey beard, black velvet cap, dark fur-trimmed robe with a heavy gold chain

props.Stage: a rough wooden stage of raw planks with a striped red and cream canopy

places.Square: Strasbourg's cobbled market square, tall half-timbered houses with steep red roofs, a round stone well in the middle

blocks.narration: This woman could not stop dancing. Not for hours. For days. It was Strasbourg, in the summer of fifteen eighteen.
blocks.visual: A woman dances alone in a medieval square

shots.visual: Frau Troffea spinning in the Square in hot afternoon sun, arms flung up, skirt flaring, eyes wide with fear
beats: she spins with her arms flung up

shots.visual: Frau Troffea still dancing alone beside the stone well of the Square at night in torchlight, exhausted, bare feet stamping
beats: her bare feet stamp the cobblestones

shots.visual: The Square in bright morning sun, half-timbered houses all around, Frau Troffea dancing alone by the well as townspeople stare from doorways
beats: she keeps spinning in the middle

blocks.narration: Within a week, dozens of strangers had joined her. By the end of summer, some accounts say hundreds were dancing.
blocks.visual: The dancing spreads through the town

shots.visual: Townspeople in plain linen clothes joining Frau Troffea in the Square one after another in the morning sun, a baker among them
beats: a baker drops his basket and starts dancing
two women join hands and spin

shots.visual: The whole Square packed with hundreds of dancing townspeople in dusty midday sun, Frau Troffea in red at the centre

blocks.narration: So the town leaders made a strange call. More dancing would cure it, they said. They built a stage and hired musicians.
blocks.visual: The town builds a stage for the dancers

shots.visual: The Magistrate on the steps of a half-timbered town hall at the edge of the Square in late afternoon light, raising one finger
beats: he points firmly down at the square

shots.visual: Workers hammering the Stage together in the Square while the Magistrate watches with folded arms
Three musicians with a drum and two pipes playing on the Stage above the dancing crowd in the Square at sunset

blocks.narration: It only got worse. Dancers collapsed in the heat, and historians still argue over how many of them actually died.

shots.visual: A tired dancer in a brown tunic sinking to his knees on the cobblestones of the Square in torchlight
beats: he sinks slowly to his knees

shots.visual: Exhausted dancers slumped against the stone well and house walls of the Square in dim torchlight, Frau Troffea still swaying among them
beats: Frau Troffea sways on, eyes half closed

blocks.narration: The leading theory: mass panic in a town crushed by famine and disease. And it all started with one woman, dancing.
blocks.visual: A starving town, and one woman begins again

shots.visual: Empty wooden grain barrels and a shuttered bakery in the Square at grey dawn, thin townspeople watching from doorways
beats: a gust rolls an empty barrel across the cobbles
a townsperson pulls a door shut

shots.visual: Frau Troffea alone in the empty Square at sunrise, lifting her arms and starting to dance again
beats: she takes her first spinning step

captions.hook_line: In 1518 a woman started dancing in the street and couldn't stop for days 💃
captions.body: In July 1518 in Strasbourg, Frau Troffea began dancing in the street. Within a week about 34 people had joined her, and some accounts put the number at around 400 within a month. The authorities built a stage and hired musicians, believing more dancing would cure it. Historians still debate the deaths; a leading explanation is mass psychogenic illness in a town hit by famine and disease.
